1415.title: Food as theology
1415.hook: the langar teaches equality through a meal
1415.howItsDone: Gurdwaras serve langar, a free vegetarian meal cooked and served by volunteers, to anyone who comes; people traditionally sit together in rows on the floor, in pangat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kesh as acceptance: the form kept whole, tended with a comb. Your line was as given.

A long strip of cloth runs down the hall floor, and people sit along it, cross-legged, in a single row. A volunteer comes down the line with a steel bucket and a ladle, and a scoop of dal lands on each tray. Then a roti, dropped into hands held open. The person on your left might be a taxi driver. On your right, a doctor, or a student, or someone who hasn't eaten since yesterday. Nobody asks. Nobody pays. The food is simple, and it's the same for everyone in the row. This is langar, and to Sikhs it's more than a free lunch. A meal can teach.
screen: `A STRIP OF CLOTH, A SINGLE ROW.` → `DAL, ROTI, OPEN HANDS.` → `A MEAL CAN TEACH.`

segments.voice: First, langar itself: the Guru's kitchen, cooked and served by volunteers and open to anyone who comes. Sikhs trace it back to Guru Nanak, and it's kept in gurdwaras to this day. Second, the Granth remembers it. In a ballad by the musicians Balwand and Satta, the langar of Guru Angad's time is praised, and so is Mata Khivi, Guru Angad's wife. In paraphrase, she is a good woman who gives cool shade like a leafy tree, and in the langar the Guru's wealth is shared out: rich kheer, made with ghee. Notice what scripture praises here: a kitchen, and the woman running it. Third, the row. The meal is eaten in pangat, sitting in a line on the same floor. In a society where rules about who could eat with whom marked people as higher and lower, sitting in one row said something without a single word. Tradition says that when the emperor Akbar came to meet Guru Amar Das, he was asked to eat in the langar first, and he sat in the row with everyone else. First the row, then the meeting. Fourth, why call this theology. Sikh teaching says the one Light is in every person. You can say that in a sermon. Or you can hand everyone the same bowl, at the same height, from the same pot, and let them notice who is sitting next to them. A belief about God becomes a seating plan.
screen: `LANGAR: THE GURU'S KITCHEN.` · `MATA KHIVI, PRAISED IN THE GRANTH.` · `PANGAT: ONE ROW, EVEN AN EMPEROR.` · `A BELIEF BECOMES A SEATING PLAN.` · then, large: `EQUALITY AT THE TABLE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people you usually eat with, then let your mind wander wider: a coworker you've never had lunch with, a neighbor, an older relative, someone whose life looks nothing like yours. Let one face come forward, and picture the two of you at the same table, same food, same height. Breathe out, and let the picture stay a while.
Food as theology. The langar teaches that the Light is in everyone by seating everyone in one row, with the same food. Today's word.
Your line: equality at the table. One row, one pot, even for an emperor. Same time tomorrow.

1416.title: Hospitality to guests
1416.hook: the guest is honored; the door stays open
1416.howItsDone: Gurdwaras welcome anyone who comes, of any faith or none, asking that visitors cover their heads and remove their shoes; Sikh households traditionally greet guests with food and tea.

segments.voice: Yesterday, food as theology: one row, one pot, even for an emperor. Your line was equality at the table.

Ji aayan nu. It's a Punjabi welcome, said at the door, sometimes with both hands pressed together, and a question follows close behind: tea? The kettle is already on. A guest arrives, and the house rearranges itself around them. The good cup comes out. Someone gives up the best chair. A small, ordinary scene, but in Sikh teaching it rests on something larger than manners. Yesterday was the meal. Today is the door, and the idea that it shouldn't be closed to anyone.
screen: `JI AAYAN NU: WELCOME.` → `THE KETTLE IS ALREADY ON.` → `TODAY, THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: First, the reason. In a hymn in Raag Majh, Guru Arjan says to God, in paraphrase, that all are called sharers in Your household, and You are seen as outside of no one. The Punjabi word is saanjhivaal: partners, people who share. If God is within everyone, then no guest is a stranger. Second, the building. The Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, the Golden Temple, is a place Sikhs hold dear, and tradition says its doors open on every side, as a sign that people from every direction are welcome. Whatever you believe, whatever you're called, there's a way in from where you're standing. Third, what the gurdwara does with that. Alongside the langar, some gurdwaras keep rooms where travelers can rest, and anyone can come in, cover their head, and sit. The guest is honored with what the house has: food, shade, a place on the floor with everyone else. Fourth, the cost. An open door isn't always comfortable. It lets in people who are loud, or sad, or not like us. Keeping it open means deciding ahead of time that whoever knocks is welcome before you know who they are. That's hard when the doorbell rings and you're tired. But it's what the hymn is pointing at: if God is outside of no one, the door has no one to close against.
screen: `SAANJHIVAAL: NO ONE IS AN OUTSIDER.` · `DOORS ON EVERY SIDE, TRADITION SAYS.` · `FOOD, SHADE, A PLACE ON THE FLOOR.` · `WELCOME BEFORE YOU KNOW WHO KNOCKS.` · then, large: `THE DOOR STAYS OPEN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who might come through your door, your inbox or your desk this week: a visitor, a new coworker, a neighbor you've only waved at. Breathe in and see them arriving; breathe out and decide, before they get there, that they're welcome, with one small thing to offer: a drink, a chair, real attention, their name said properly. If you pray, hold them in your prayer.
Hospitality to guests. The guest is honored because, as Guru Arjan sings, all are sharers, and God is outside of no one. Today's word.
Your line: the door stays open. Doors on every side, a way in from anywhere. Until tomorrow.

1417.title: Honest citizenship
1417.hook: Sikhs take part honestly in the life of their countries
1417.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of kirat karni, earning an honest living, and of seva beyond the gurdwara, which can mean volunteering, serving food in times of need, and taking part in the life of their towns and countries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hospitality to guests: saanjhivaal, all are sharers, and God is outside of no one. Your line was the door stays open.

A jury summons arrives in a plain envelope, and the first thought is how to get out of it. A form asks you to report every bit of income, and there's a small line you could leave blank. A ballot sits on the counter for a week. Nobody will make a film about filling in a form truthfully. But this is where a lot of public life actually happens: small, boring moments where honesty costs a little and nobody's watching. Sikh teaching has something to say about them, and it starts with a line that ranks something above truth itself.
screen: `A JURY SUMMONS, A FORM, A BALLOT.` → `SMALL, BORING, UNWATCHED.` → `ONE STEP FURTHER.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In Sri Raag, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: truth is higher than everything, but higher still is truthful living. Not just believing what's true; living it, in the dull places. A truthful life includes the tax form. Second, kirat. Sikh teaching asks for an honest living, kirat karni. In a hymn in Raag Sarang, Guru Nanak says the one who eats what they've earned by their own effort, and gives some of it away with their own hand, knows the way. Earn honestly, share freely: a good neighbor and a good citizen in one sentence. Third, wherever they live. Sikhs live in many places and take part in public life in many ways: as soldiers and nurses, teachers and drivers, voters and volunteers. You may have seen Sikh volunteers cooking for strangers after a storm or a flood. That's langar leaving the gurdwara and walking into the street. Faith here isn't kept apart from the town; it's how you show up in it. Fourth, the small duties. Honest citizenship is mostly unglamorous. Answering the summons. Filling the form truthfully. Paying the fine you actually owe. Voting, or helping someone get to the polls. Picking up the litter outside your own door. None of these is a sermon. Each one is truthful living, the thing Guru Nanak placed higher still, tested at the kitchen counter, not the podium.
screen: `TRUTHFUL LIVING IS HIGHER STILL.` · `KIRAT: EARN HONESTLY, SHARE FREELY.` · `LANGAR WALKS INTO THE STREET.` · `THE FORM, THE SUMMONS, THE BALLOT.` · then, large: `HONEST CITIZENS.`

segments.voice: Let the small public things you've been putting off run past, a form, a bill, a neighbor's request, a broken streetlight to report, and let one rise to the top. Breathe in and admit, honestly and without blame, why you've avoided it. Breathe out and picture yourself doing it fully, even the part nobody would check.
Honest citizenship. Truthful living, which Guru Nanak placed higher than truth alone, carried into the form, the summons and the street. Today's word.
Your line: honest citizens. Langar walks out of the gurdwara and into the street. Rest well.

1418.title: Thinking as a Sikh today
1418.howItsDone: Gurdwaras read a hukamnama, a hymn taken from where the Guru Granth Sahib opens, as the order of the day; Sikhs also discuss new questions together, and Sikh bodies such as the Akal Takht sometimes issue guidance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, honest citizenship: truthful living, higher than truth alone, carried into the form and the street. Your line was honest citizens.

What would the Gurus say about a phone that never stops buzzing? About a machine that can write a hymn? About medicine that can keep a body breathing long after the person seems gone? About a planet getting warmer? None of these questions existed when the hymns were sung. The Granth never mentions a screen. And yet Sikhs carry these questions into the gurdwara all the same, right past the shoes left at the door. So how do you think with an old book about a new world, without pretending it says what it doesn't?
screen: `A PHONE, A MACHINE, A WARMING PLANET.` → `THE GRANTH NEVER MENTIONS A SCREEN.` → `AN OLD BOOK, A NEW WORLD.`

segments.voice: First, the Granth asks for thinking. In Raag Asa, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that when learning is truly reflected on, a person becomes a help to others. The word is vichar: reflection, turning a teaching over until it's yours. Reading isn't the end; thinking it through is part of the practice. Second, a daily habit. Each day in the gurdwara, the Granth is opened and a hymn read from where it opens. That reading is the hukamnama, the order of the day. Sikhs bring whatever they're carrying to it, and then sit with what comes back: an old Word speaking into a new morning. Third, the community. When a new question touches the whole Sikh community, Sikh bodies such as the Akal Takht in Amritsar sometimes speak to it. Sikhs also talk, write and sometimes disagree, in homes and gurdwaras and online. Thinking as a Sikh today is done in company. Fourth, principle, not proof-text. There's no verse about phones. But there are threads you've met all year: remember the Name, work honestly, share, the Light in everyone, the good of all. Hold a new question up to those, and it starts to sort itself. Does this tool help me remember, or only forget? Does this choice treat everyone as carrying the same Light? Old word, new question, and the patience to let them meet.

segments.voice: Let one real question come up, something the old world never faced, a choice about screens, money, work or a relative's care, and say it to yourself plainly. Then hold it up to one thread per breath: remembering, honest work, sharing, the good of all. Notice which thread tugs, and stay with it.
Thinking as a Sikh today. Vichar, reflection, bringing new questions to the old Word, with the community and the day's hukamnama. Today's word.

1419.title: Sikh thought close
1419.hook: God, the self, ethics and the world, through the Guru's eyes
1419.howItsDone: Sikhs study Gurmat, the Guru's teaching, through the Guru Granth Sahib, katha (talks explaining the hymns) in the gurdwara, and daily prayers such as the Japji, whose first pauri asks how to become truthful.

segments.voice: Yesterday, thinking as a Sikh today: vichar, the hukamnama, and principle before proof-text. Your line was old word, new questions.

Some of what we learn slips away by the end of the week. Some ideas don't. They lodge somewhere, like a pebble in a shoe, and you keep noticing them at odd moments: in traffic, at the sink, halfway through an argument. This stretch of the path has been about Sikh thought: what the Gurus taught about God, about the self, about how to live, and about the world we share. Today it closes. Not with a test. With a walk back through the rooms, and a question at the end: which idea came home with you?
screen: `A PEBBLE IN A SHOE.` → `GOD, SELF, LIVING, WORLD.` → `WHICH IDEA CAME HOME WITH YOU?`

segments.voice: First, God. The Granth opens with Ik Onkar, the One, and you met the names: Waheguru, the Wonderful Lord, and many others drawn from many tongues. You met God with qualities and without, vast and close, beyond everything and within everyone. Second, the self. Haumai, ego, which isn't the same as you. The mind as a friend to be trained, not an enemy to be beaten. Hukam, the order, and effort inside it. Grace and deeds. This life as the chance, and the hope of being free while still living. Third, how to live. The thieves that clutch and crave: attachment, greed, desire out of place. Against them, chardi kala, rising spirits, and bhaana, accepting the will. Ardas that asks and then accepts. The portrait of the Gurmukh, humble and truthful and serving, and of the Khalsa. Fourth, the world. Equal souls. Women as equals. Force only as the last resort, justice for the wronged, truth spoken to rulers. Then the week just gone: many tongues in one script, the Word that is sung, kesh as given, the langar row, the open door, honest citizens, old words meeting new questions. Underneath it all sits the question Guru Nanak asks in the first pauri of the Japji. In paraphrase: how do we become truthful, and how does the wall of falsehood come down? His answer: by walking in the hukam, the order written with us. Much of this stretch can be heard as unpacking that line.
screen: `GOD: ONE, NAMED IN MANY WAYS.` · `THE SELF: EGO, MIND, FREE WHILE LIVING.` · `LIVING: THIEVES, RISING SPIRITS, THE GURMUKH.` · `THE WORLD: EQUAL SOULS, AN OPEN DOOR.` · then, large: `THE IDEA THAT STAYED.`

segments.voice: Let the rooms go by slowly: God, the self, how to live, the world. Don't pick the idea you think you should; wait for the one that has quietly been showing up in your days, the pebble in the shoe, and give it a name in a few words. If you pray, offer thanks for it; if you don't, just hold it, and let it stay.
Sikh thought close. God, the self, how to live and the world, through the Guru's eyes, gathered under one question: how does the wall of falsehood come down? Today's word.
Your line: the idea that stayed. A pebble in the shoe, carried home. A stretch of Sikh thought, closed.

1420.title: Looking back: the ragas
1420.howItsDone: In gurdwaras, ragis (kirtan musicians) sing hymns in the raga named at their head, and Sikh practice sets particular hymns, such as Asa di Var in the morning, for particular times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the close of Sikh thought: God, the self, how to live and the world. Your line was the idea that stayed.

Some songs belong to a time of day. A lullaby at noon sounds wrong. A wedding song at a funeral would be unbearable. The Sikh tradition built that into the scripture itself. Over the year you've met hymns of praise, of longing, of warning, of joy, each under a heading that named its raga before anything else. So as this year of the ways of the Guru begins to close, the looking back starts with the sound under the words: how it was meant to be heard.
screen: `A LULLABY AT NOON SOUNDS WRONG.` → `THE YEAR BEGINS TO CLOSE.` → `HOW IT WAS MEANT TO BE HEARD.`

segments.voice: First, the headings. You met this a week ago: after the opening prayers, the Guru Granth Sahib is arranged by raga. The hymns sat under raga names, like a door you walk through before you hear a word. Second, a raga is a mood. Musicians in the tradition speak of each one having its own color and its own hour. In Sikh practice, Asa di Var is sung in the early morning. Tradition links Basant with spring and Malar with the rains. The Word doesn't change, but it arrives dressed for the moment. Third, the moods are honest. The Granth doesn't stay cheerful. In Raag Tukhari, Guru Nanak's song of the months walks through the year as a bride longing for her beloved: the heat, the rain, the cold, each month its own ache, until union comes. Longing gets its own music. So does warning, so does celebration. Nobody is asked to fake a mood they're not in. Fourth, one Word, many moods. The same Name is sung in grief and in joy, at dawn and at night, in spring and in the rains. There's a raga for whatever state you walk in with, which means no mood has to be fixed before coming near the Word. You bring the mood. The music meets it.

1421.title: Looking back: the Gurus' teachings
1421.hook: Nanak's dialogues, the Gurus' voices, the Ninth's calm
1421.tomorrow: Looking back: the Tenth Guru's pen
1421.howItsDone: Sikhs read and sing the hymns of the Gurus and the bhagats together in the Guru Granth Sahib; each hymn's heading names its raga and its Mahala, which tells readers which Guru composed it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the ragas: one Word sung in every mood. Your line was many moods.

In a hymn by Guru Nanak, there's his name: Nanak. In a hymn by Guru Arjan, a later Guru, the same name appears: Nanak. Guru Amar Das, Guru Ram Das, Guru Tegh Bahadur: the Gurus whose hymns fill the Granth sign them as Nanak. To a newcomer, it can look like a mistake in the credits. To Sikhs, it's the point. After the music, the voices: how different they sound, and why they're signed with one name.
screen: `SIGNED: NANAK.` → `A DIFFERENT GURU, THE SAME NAME.` → `NOT A MISTAKE. THE POINT.`

segments.voice: First, Nanak in dialogue. Guru Nanak doesn't only sing; he argues, gently. In the Sidh Gosht, yogis who have left the world question him: why stay among householders? His answers keep returning to the Word, and to living truthfully in the world rather than fleeing it. Teaching, for him, could be a conversation. Second, how you tell the voices apart. Each hymn carries a heading, Mahala one, Mahala two and so on, marking which Guru composed it, while the signature stays Nanak. Listen across them: Guru Angad's spare sloks, Guru Amar Das's Anand, Guru Arjan's long Sukhmani. Different temperaments. One signature. Third, the Ninth Guru's calm. Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns have a stillness all their own. In Raag Sorath he describes, in paraphrase, the person who isn't shaken by pain, isn't carried off by pleasure, holds praise and blame alike, and sees gold as dust. It reads like the voice of someone who has already let go. Fourth, why one name. In the ballad of Balwand and Satta, they sing, in paraphrase, that the light was the same and the way was the same; only the body changed. Sikhs understand the Gurus as one light passing from lamp to lamp. And around them, the bhagats, Kabir, Farid, Namdev and others, keep their own names, welcomed in. Many voices, saying the truth in their own way, without needing to drown each other out.
screen: `NANAK IN DIALOGUE: THE SIDH GOSHT.` · `MAHALA: WHICH GURU IS SPEAKING.` · `THE NINTH GURU'S CALM.` · `ONE LIGHT, LAMP TO LAMP.` · then, large: `MANY VOICES.`

segments.voice: Here are three teachings from three voices, in paraphrase. Guru Nanak: stay in the world, and live truthfully in it; Guru Arjan: all are sharers, and God is outside of no one; Guru Tegh Bahadur: hold praise and blame alike. Let one of them choose you, and say it slowly, once on the in-breath, once on the out-breath.
Looking back. At the year's close, the Gurus' teachings: different voices, each hymn marked by its Mahala, all signed Nanak, one light passed on. Today's word.
Your line: many voices. One light, passed on from lamp to lamp. See you tomorrow.
